title: Nanocomposite catalyst of graphitic carbon nitride and Cu/Fe mixed metal oxide for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO
abstract: To address the challenges of excessive emission of CO2, development of highly efficient electrocatalysts based on earth-abundant metals and non-metals for CO2 reduction is of great importance. Herein, we report a novel gC3N4/Cu2O-FeO heterogeneous nanocomposite catalyst for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO, with a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 84.4 % at a low onset overpotential of -0.24 V vs. normal hydrogen electrode (NHE). Moreover, the turnover frequency for CO2 conversion to CO reached 10300 h 1 with a high selectivity of 96.3 % at -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl, corresponding to a thermodynamic overpotential of -0.865 V vs. NHE. The excellent CO2 reduction to CO can be attributed to the intimate interfacial interaction between the g-C3N4 and metal oxides (Cu2O-FeO) and the higher electrochemically active surface area. Therefore, this work demonstrates the use of a g-C3N4/mixed metal oxide heterostructure as a novel and efficient nanocomposite for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction in neutral aqueous medium.

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Electrocatalysis Carbon dioxide reduction Composite materials Oxygen vacancies Graphitic carbon nitride Metal oxides
A B S T R A C T
To address the challenges of excessive emission of CO2, development of highly efficient electrocatalysts based on earth-abundant metals and non-metals for CO2 reduction is of great importance. Herein, we report a novel gC3N4/Cu2O-FeO heterogeneous nanocomposite catalyst for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO, with a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 84.4 % at a low onset overpotential of -0.24 V vs. normal hydrogen electrode (NHE). Moreover, the turnover frequency for CO2 conversion to CO reached 10300 h− 1 with a high selectivity of 96.3 % at -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl, corresponding to a thermodynamic overpotential of -0.865 V vs. NHE. The excellent CO2 reduction to CO can be attributed to the intimate interfacial interaction between the g-C3N4 and metal oxides (Cu2O-FeO) and the higher electrochemically active surface area. Therefore, this work demonstrates the use of a g-C3N4/mixed metal oxide heterostructure as a novel and efficient nanocomposite for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction in neutral aqueous medium.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
As the primary greenhouse gas, CO2 is believed to play a crucial role in global warming. The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere keeps rising with the increase in fossil fuel combustion, thus inducing climate change and raising sea level [1,2]. Various studies have been carried out on artificial photosynthesis for CO2 reduction using sunlight as the main energy input [3]. To date, effective methods such as thermochemical[4], photocatalytic, photoelectrochemical [5,6], and electrochemical methods [7,8] have been applied to reduce CO2 concentration. Nonetheless, photocatalytic CO2 reduction mostly suffers from very limited efficiency and poor selectivity [9,10]. Alternatively, direct electrochemical CO2 reductions into hydrocarbons or CO have advantages over photocatalytic systems as they operate under ambient conditions at high reaction rates with good efficiencies, and use environmentally friendly aqueous electrolytes [11].
The CO2 electro-reduction reaction, in which CO production proceeds according to Eq. (1), is a process of fundamental importance [12]. The product, ‘CO’, is an important feedstock for synthesis of methanol [13], formic acid [14], ethanol [15] etc., ultimately storing electricity in the form of chemical energy. Extensive experimental works have been carried out on the electrochemical CO2 reduction using metals (Cu, Sn,
Ag, etc.) [16], metal oxides (Cu2O, ZnO, etc.) [17], nanosheets [18], chalcogenides [19], carbon-based materials [20], and graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) [21] to convert CO2 into different products via electrocatalysis.
CO2 + 2e− + 2H+ → CO + H2O (1)
Among these, g-C3N4 has recently received considerable attention due to its high stability under severe chemical conditions, larger surface area, and low cost, which makes it a suitable heterogeneous catalyst for electrocatalytic water oxidation [22] and hydrogen evolution [23]. g-C3N4 can be readily prepared by thermal polymerization of cheap precursors, such as dicyanamide [24], melamine [25], or thiourea [26]. To obtain such composite materials, g-C3N4 can be incorporated with transition metal oxides, e.g. Cu2O, which create an electric field to provide a strong driving force for charge migration between Cu2O and g-C3N4 in order to accelerate the redox processes in the p-n heterojunctions [27]. There are only few reports examining metal-free g-C3N4 materials as catalysts for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. In 2018, Li et al. reported ultrathin two-dimensional g-C3N4 for electrochemical CO2 reduction. Their catalyst achieved a maximum Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 80 % for CO. However, this catalyst has a relatively large Tafel slope

and less current density of 3.05 mA/cm2 [28]. In a similar report by R. Amal et al., g-C3N4 was combined with multi-wall carbon nanotubes for the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to achieve 60 % FEs for CO production at an applied potential of -0.75 V vs. RHE [21].
Hybrid materials using 2D materials (e.g., carbon materials [20] and g-C3N4 [28]) incorporated with metals or metal oxides catalysts for CO2 reductions have also been examined in order to reach low overpotential, high product selectivity, and large current densities [29,30]. These objectives could potentially be achieved by tuning the morphology and size of the nanostructures of each component or doping heteroatoms to the hybrid materials [31]. Lu et al. reported Ag-decorated sulfur-doped graphitic carbon nitride/carbon nanotube nanocomposites (Ag-S-C3N4 /CNT) for electrochemical CO2 reduction. A maximum FE of over 91.4 % with a Tafel slope of 136 mV/dec was achieved in an H-type cell assembly [30]. More recently, heterostructures containing oxides of a non-noble metal, such as iron [32] or copper [33] have attracted much attention because they are earth-abundant and can provide low cost hybrid material. Importantly, integrating g-C3N4 with such nanosized particles results in stable materials that could function as active electrochemical catalysts for CO2 reduction [34]. However, to date, no report is available in the literature on the electrocatalytic performance of mixed metallic oxides consisting of Cu2O-FeO supported on g-C3N4.
Herein, we synthesized a g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO heterostructure nanocomposite in two steps, a thermal polymerization followed by a hydrothermal synthetic pathway. The performance of the electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction is evaluated in terms of its catalytic activity, long-term stability, and product selectivity in a simple one-pot assembly in a threeelectrode electrochemical cell. The g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO heterostructure showed an excellent activity for CO formation with a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 84.4 % at an applied potential of -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl to achieve a turnover frequency (TOF) of 10,300 h− 1 and CO/H2 selectivity of 26:1, which is a significant improvement compared with the previously metal-free or Ag-decorated S-doped reports [28,29]. The synergistic effect was achieved via significant enrichments in electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) and oxygen deficiencies in the mixed metal oxides of Cu2O-FeO, which improved the kinetics of the electrons that reached at reaction surface and enhanced catalytic performance of g-C3N4 hybrid materials in an aqueous electrolyte at neutral pH.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Dicyandiamide (Acros Organics, 99.5 %), ethanol, methanol, Nafion® perfluorinated resin solution (5 wt. % in lower aliphatic alcohols and water, contains 15–20 % water), copper acetate monohydrate (Cu(CH3COO)2•H2O, 99 %), iron(III) acetylacetonate (Fe(C5H7O2)3, 99 %), potassium chloride (99 %), triethylene glycol (99 %), CO2 gas (99.999 %) were used as received.

sections.heading: 2.2. Preparation of bulk g-C3N4
sections.text: Bulk g-C3N4 was synthesized using a modified procedure by Xia et al. [35]. Dicyandiamide (2 g, 23.79 mmol) was placed in a crucible and heated to 350 ◦C at the rate of 4 ◦C/min in a muffle furnace. The temperature was maintained for 2 h, then the heating was continued to reach 600 ◦C at the rate of 3 ◦C/min for 2 h more. After cooling down, the yellow powder product was collected and labeled as bulk g-C3N4 (B-GCN).

sections.heading: 2.3. Preparation of g-C3N4 nano sheets
sections.text:
The as prepared B-GCN (1 g) was mixed with 10 mL of H2SO4 (98 wt. %) in a round-bottom flask and stirred for 8 h at room temperature. The mixture was slowly poured into 100 mL of deionized water and
sonicated for exfoliation for 2 h. The obtained suspension was centrifuged and the collected solid was washed thoroughly with deionized water then dried at 60 ◦C in a vacuum oven overnight. The obtained powder (0.5 g) was added in a flask with 150 mL of methanol and refluxed in an oil bath heater at 65 ◦C for 6 h. After centrifugation and drying at 60 ◦C in a vacuum oven, the obtained product was labeled as graphitic carbon nitride, g-C3N4 [36].

sections.heading: 2.4. Synthesis for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO nanocomposite
sections.text: The nanocomposite of graphitic carbon nitride and Cu2O-FeO (gC3N4/Cu2O-FeO) was synthesized according to Zhang et al. in which 100 mg of the prepared g-C3N4, 60 mg of copper(II) acetate monohydrate, and 40 mg of iron(III) acetylacetonate in a weight ratio of 5:3:2 were added into a 60 mL triethylene glycol. The solution was sonicated for 30 min and transferred into a Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave and reacted at 200 ◦C for 12 h. After cooling down to room temperature, the obtained precipitate was centrifuged, washed with ethanol and dried in a vacuum oven at 60 ◦C for overnight, and labeled as g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO [37]. The preparation of mixed copper and iron oxide nanoparticles followed procedures similar to that of g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO composites without the addition of g-C3N4 and the product was labeled as Cu2O-FeO.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text: The structure, composition and chemical states of the g-C3N4/Cu2OFeO, Cu2O-FeO, and g-C3N4 were investigated by transmission electron microscope (TEM), scanning electron microscope (SEM), X-ray powder diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR). Their CO2 reduction activities were evaluated under electrochemical conditions, and the reaction products were quantified by gas chromatography with Thermal Conductivity Detector(TCD).

sections.heading: 3.1. Electron microscope analysis
sections.text:
To confirm the morphology and elemental composition, TEM and SEM images of the composite materials were recorded. The pristine gC3N4 matrix adopts a transparent sheet-like morphology indicating layered nature of the nanosheet as seen in Figs. S1 and S2. As shown in Figs. 1a–c and S3, small Cu2O and FeO composite particles (~10 nm) deposited on the interfaces of g-C3N4 nanosheets can be clearly visualized from the HR-TEM images of g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO, and confirms the formation of a heterostructure nanocomposite materials. The elemental mapping and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) images of gC3N4/Cu2O-FeO (Figs. 1d–i and S4) demonstrated that the nanocomposite exhibits a well-dispersed C and N elements and evenly distributed Cu, Fe, and O elements over g-C3N4 nanosheet plates.
The composition of the two metals, Fe and Cu was further quantified by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) mass spectrometry (Table S1). The obtained weight ratio of 1:2.5 after the deposition of Cu2O-FeO on gC3N4, is in good agreement with Fe/Cu theoretical weight ratio of 1:1.28. Consistent results as summarized in Table S2 were also obtained by EDX from TEM (weight ratio of 1:2.19 and atomic ratio of 1:1.92, Fig. S4 in SI) and SEM (weight ratio of 1:2.17 and atomic ratio of 1:1.90). The particle size distribution histogram as shown in supporting Fig. S5 indicates that the mean size of the particles is 3.4 ± 0.98 nm. As displayed in Fig. S6, the lattice spacings of the two domains were measured to be 0.24 and 0.30 nm using HRTEM. These lattice spacings correspond to the (111) and (011) planes of FeO [38] and Cu2O [39], respectively. The d-spacing value of 0.24 nm is in close agreement with the value obtained from powder X-ray diffraction (0.25 nm) with only 4 % difference (Table S3). These measurements confirmed the well-dispersed nature of mixed metal oxides in the composite materials.

sections.heading: 3.2. X-ray photoemission (XPS) and X-ray absorption (XAS) spectroscopic measurements
sections.text:
To obtain more information about the elemental composition, the XPS spectra for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO are obtained as survey scan displayed in Fig. 2a, whilst, Fig. 2b–f shows the composed transitions from different elements and their peak deconvolution results.
The peaks for C 1s (Fig. 2b) with binding energies (BEs) of 284.9 and 288.2 eV were attributed to standard reference carbon and N=C(N)-N [40], respectively. An additional peak around 286.3 eV was ascribed to N-C=N carbons connected to two nitrogen atoms on g-C3N4 [41]. The dominant peak at 398.7 eV for N 1s corresponded to the two coordinated sp2-bonded N (C=N-C) involved in the heptazine rings, while the peak at 399.6 eV was attributed to the N atoms bridging three carbon atoms in g-C3N4 and the weak peak at 401.3 eV indicated the presence of N-H groups on the edge of the heptazine network (Fig. 2c) [42]. Visibly, the characteristic peak shown in Fig. 2d of the Cu 2p3/2 at 932.5 eV was attributed to the Cu+ [43] and the weak peak of Cu2+ at 933.2 eV [44] might be due to a partial oxidation of Cu2O. For Fe, the peak at 710.9 eV was assigned to ferrous 2p3/2 photoelectron peak and a weaker peak at 712.3 eV was ascribed to ferric species [45]. As shown in Fig. 2f, the peak at 530.1 eV was ascribed to O 1s of metal oxides [46]. The peaks with BEs at 531.7 eV and 533.2 eV for O 1s were assigned to O2 adsorbed on oxygen deficiency regions (Ov) and chemisorbed oxygen (Oc) from H2O adsorbed at the surface of oxygen vacancy sites, respectively [47, 48]. Noticeably, the shifts in O 1s deconvoluted peaks to higher binding energies suggest the presence of surface oxygen vacancies [49] (Fig. S7), which might enhance the overall catalytic efficiencies of
g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO through substrate trapping and increase the lifetime of reducing equivalents [50]. In addition, the observations of slight shifts in the binding energies of C1 s and N1 s (Figs. S8 and 9 in SI) further confirm intimate interactions between g-C3N4 surfaces and Cu2O-FeO in the composite materials [51].
To elaborate the local structure and interactions between g-C3N4 and Cu2O-FeO in more detail, we performed X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopic measurements for C, N and O elements (Figs. S10 and 11). Carbon K-edge spectra revealed that the intensity of peak associated with carbon species at 286.6 eV (π*(C-O)) increased after the incorporation of Cu2O-FeO, suggesting perturbations of carbon orbitals that resulted from electronic interactions between Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4. Similarly, the N K-edge spectrum showed a 1 s to π* transition at 402.2 eV and a broad peak at >408 eV attributed to C-N conjugated double bonds. Enhancement in peak intensity of N K-edge spectrum implies charge transfer from N sites to Cu2O-FeO via orbital hybridizations between g-C3N4 and Cu2O-FeO, pointing to the synergistic effect in the composite materials [52]. Likewise, the O K-edge spectrum for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO was similar to those of Cu2O-FeO, Cu2O, and FeO, indicating similar electronic environment and oxidation states (Fig. S11). However, a slight shift of the absorption edge to a lower energy for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO was observed indicating an increase in oxygen vacancy concentration [53]. Thus, XANES spectrum confirms the intimate interactions between g-C3N4 surfaces and Cu2O-FeO in the composite materials which is beneficial to the catalytic performance [50].

sections.heading: 3.3. Powder X-ray diffraction and FT-IR measurements
sections.text:
To further confirm their structures and phases, the XRD patterns of the as-synthesized g-C3N4, Cu2O-FeO, and g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO were collected and presented in Fig. 3a. The peaks were matched with Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD). The strong peak located at 27.48◦ in g-C3N4 belongs to the typical (002) interlayer stacking plane of the conjugated g-C3N4. On the other hand, the peak at 12.78◦ is an inplane structural packing of carbon nitride originating from (100) plane [54]. The mixed copper and iron oxide nanoparticles, Cu2O-FeO, showed diffraction peaks at 2θ values of 36.47, 42.3, 61.37, and 73.5◦, which could be indexed to (111), (002), (022), and (113) planes of Cu2O
(ICSD #150886). Furthermore, the minor peak at 50.30◦ is assigned to (115) plane of Cu2O (ICSD #52043). The peaks at 36.4, 42.27, and 61.33◦ are assigned as the (101), (012), and (110) plane of FeO (ICSD #24698). Therefore, XRD data further identified Cu2O and FeO as the composition of mixed metal oxide.
The observed peaks in the XRD pattern of g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO at 2θ values of 36.5, 42.48, 61.33, and 73.5◦ correspond to (111), (002), (022) and (113) planes of Cu2O. The peak at 50.30◦ is due to (115) plane of CuO2 (ICSD 98-010-3173) and the peaks observed at 36.4, 42.27, and 61.33◦ for Cu2O-FeO were ascribed as the (101), (012), and (110) plane of FeO, respectively. The intensities of the g-C3N4 peak decreased significantly after the incorporation of Cu2O-FeO. The oveall XRD
G.W. Woyessa et al.

pattern indicates the successful formation of a g-C3N4 and mixed metal oxide heterostructure nanocomposite which is in agreement with XPS and EDX mapping. The interactions between different constituents in the samples of g-C3N4, Cu2O-FeO, and g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO were further probed by FTIR as shown in Fig. 3b. The broad band at 3000− 3500 cm− 1 in the samples of g-C3N4 and g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO belongs to the adsorbed water molecules and the peak at 810 cm− 1 is attributed to the breathing ring vibrational mode of the heptazine units. The peaks at 1637, 1407, 1320, and 1239 cm-1are characteristics of the skeletal stretching vibrational modes of C=N and C-N(-C)-C heptazine moieties [55]. The broad peaks at 580− 650 cm− 1 in both the samples of Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO are attributed to the stretching vibrations of the Cu-O bonds of Cu2O [56] and Fe-O of FeO [57]. The decrease in the intensity of IR-absorption in the region 600− 650 cm− 1 for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO
confirms the formation of oxygen vacancies as shown in Fig. S12 of SI [58,59]. Noticeably, both the FT-IR results and XPS data indicate the presence of non-stoichiometric oxygen deficient sites in g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO.

sections.heading: 3.4. Electrochemical property, cyclic voltammetry and Tafel plots of the catalysts
sections.text:
All electrochemical CO2 reduction reactions including cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements, linear sweep voltammetry, and bulk electrolysis were conducted in aqueous solution (15 mL) containing 0.1 M KCl as electrolyte on an electrochemical workstation (CHI-660E) using a three-electrode system with the catalyst, g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO, coated on an FTO glass as the working electrodes, Ag/AgCl as the
G.W. Woyessa et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120052
reference electrode, and platinum wire as auxiliary electrode (Fig. S13). The working electrodes with g-C3N4 or Cu2O-FeO coated on FTO were also used for electrochemical CO2 reductions as a control. KCl was chosen as electrolyte since it increases CO2 solubility and discourages H2 evolution [60].
The CO2 reduction efficiency of the catalysts on FTO scaffold has been examined by sweeping the applied voltage between 0 and − 2 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). For CV measurements, the active area on working electrodes coated with catalysts was controlled to be 1 cm x 2.5 cm while the mass density of all catalysts on working electrodes are controlled to be around 0.6 mg/cm2. As shown in Fig. 4a, the voltammogram using working electrode coated with g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO showed a significantly larger current enhancement between -0.5 and -2.0 V in a solution saturated with CO2 than saturated with N2. Furthermore, the cyclic voltammograms in Fig. 4b recorded in the presence of CO2 using g-C3N4/Cu2OFeO showed a more enhanced current density than those with g-C3N4 or Cu2O-FeO alone when potential swept to values more negative than -1.0 V. These observations indicate that CO2 reduction occurs at a sufficiently negative potential [61]. Noticeably, the blank FTO exhibits a low current density suggesting its inactivity towards CO2 reduction. The enhanced activity of CO2 reduction using the composite materials can be ascribed to the intimate interfacial contacts between g-C3N4 and the binary metal oxide, Cu2O-FeO, and the well-dispersed Cu2O-FeO nanoparticles on 2D g-C3N4 which provides a synergistic eff ;ect to enhance the CO2 reduction activity [34].
To gain a deeper insight into the kinetics of electrochemical CO2 reduction, Tafel plots were recorded as shown in Fig. 4c. The obtained Tafel slope of 116 mV/dec obtained from the voltammogram with gC3N4/Cu2O-FeO as the catalyst is less than 118 mV/dec, which suggests that the rate-determining step (RDS) is the fast-initial electron transfer [62]. Therefore, Tafel plot confirms that the catalytic surfaces can stabilize the CO2 intermediate (Eq. (2)). In contrast, the larger Tafel slopes for g-C3N4 (195 mV/dec) and Cu2O-FeO (162 mV/dec) limit the electrocatalytic mechanism on its surface where CO2 diffusion process dominates the reaction pathway [28].
From previous studies on electrochemical CO2 reduction, the following reaction pathways was considered (Eqs. (2)–(4)) [15].
CO2 + e− ↔ *CO2− (2)
CO2(g) + H+(aq) + e− → *COOH (3)
*COOH + H+(aq) + e− → *CO + H2O(l) (4)
*CO→ CO(g) (5)
Where * denotes the adsorbed molecule on electrode. The Tafel slopes, together with onset potentials, onset overpotentials
(ηon) and electrochemical active surface area (ECAS) calculated from cyclic voltammograms at different scan rates are summarized in Table 1. Electrodes coated with Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO demonstrated larger ECAS values of 1.11 cm2 and 1.28 cm2, respectively, in comparison to g-C3N4 of 0.6 cm2, which could be due to the binary metal oxide nanoparticles scattering on g-C3N4 nanosheets to provide a large number of catalytic active sites resulting in an enhanced catalytic activity [63,64]. Additionally, the higher exchange current density of 65 μA/cm2 observed in g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO than the rest, i.e. g-C3N4 (2.56 nA/cm2)
and Cu2O-FeO (3.36 μA/cm2), suggests a more facile current density flowing in equilibrium and thus a higher catalytic activity [30]. Furthermore, the onset overpotential of the nanocomposite was measured to be − 235 mV. This significantly lower onset overpotential makes the g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO electrode a suitable catalyst for electrochemical CO2 reduction. Worth mentioning, oxygen vacancies created on the mixed metal oxide might enhance the CO2 adsorption and enhance CO2 reduction activities by facilitating the formation of active anionic CO2 radical species at these sites [65]. Importantly, all the electrodes showed good stability as the charge accumulated linearly during the 18-h electrolysis (Fig. 4d).

sections.heading: 3.5. Product analysis for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO, Cu2O-FeO, and GCN
sections.text:
The products from the electro-catalytic CO2 reduction using g-C3N4/ Cu2O-FeO, Cu2O-FeO, and g-C3N4 on FTO glass as the working electrode were quantified by gas chromatography. As shown in Fig. 5a–d, the product distributions indicate that both CO and H2 are formed at an applied potential of -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl. Using g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO as the catalyst, the amount of CO increases over time and reaches a plateau after 4.5 h with an accumulated amount of 190 μmol. This value is significantly higher than around 63 μmol of CO production for both the Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4. Noticeably, the production of H2 is effectively suppressed at -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl except that g-C3N4 accumulated about 45 μmol of H2 in 4.5 h. To get a better understanding of the voltage dependencies, the FEs of CO and H2 were plotted at various potentials and presented in Fig. 5b-c. Upon increasing applied potential, the FE of CO with g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO as the catalyst reaches a maximum value of 85 % at -1.60 V with only about 4 % of H2 detected which signifies the near exclusive product selectivity achieved at -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl. The overpotential calculated at maximum FE was thus -0.865 V vs. NHE. In stark contrast, the FEs of CO only reached 47 % and 18 % at -1.60 V for Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4, respectively. The FEs of CO and H2 using different catalysts with error bar obtained from three independent catalytic runs are shown in Fig. S14 of SI.
Noticeably, as shown in Fig. 5b-c, the results of total FEs, i.e. FEs of CO plus H2, which is less than 100 % as well as the decrease of FE with an extended electrolysis in Fig. 5d both imply the formation of unidentified CO2 reduction products. Efforts have been attempted to trap the products with no success yet, although we do observe the formation of small amount of formic acid and methanol in the NMR spectra of the catalytic products. Furthermore, we postulate that water reduction accompanying with accumulated OH− under high applied potential and extended reaction time will shift the equilibrium of CO2towards HCO3− , and CO32− . It is known that both HCO3− and CO32− are much difficult to be reduced, and the dissolution of CO2 would not be fast enough to compensate for the loss of CO2 and ultimately lowering the total FE of CO plus H2 [66].
The partial current density for CO (jCO) generation obtained with the three catalysts in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KCl with an applied potential of -1.60 V are presented in Fig. 6a. The jCO obtained with the g-C3N4/Cu2OFeO is the highest among all catalysts tested herein (3.91 mA/cm2). In contrast, the values of jCO obtained with both Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4 are lower, with merely 2.19 mA/cm2 and 0.83 mA/cm2, respectively. This observation indicates that the majority of electrons consumed by C3N4/ Cu2O-FeO are used for the evolution of CO, rather than reducing protons into H2 as indicated by the low FEs and low partial current densities of H2 as shown in Figs. 5d and S15.

We further calculated the turnover frequency (TOF) of CO for different catalysts (Fig. 6b). The TOF for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO reached 10300 h− 1 which outperformed Cu2O-FeO (7340 h− 1) and g-C3N4 (4630 h− 1). Herein, the TOFs was obtained from the ratio of CO production (mole cm-2) and surface coverage ‘Γ’ (mole cm-2) per unit time obtained

indirectly from integrated area of the reduction peak from Eq. (6) (details in SI). The resulting g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO electrode shows no significant structural change, and the corresponding SEM images gave further confirmation that the compositions of the catalyst were unchanged even after 18 h (Fig. S16). The cyclability for the catalyst was also monitored. All the three catalysts maintained almost similar FEs even after 3 consecutive runs (Fig. S17).
The comparison of the Faradic efficiencies of different electrocatalysts for selective CO2 reduction to CO is presented in Table 2. The Faradic efficiencies of the current research work dictate that the catalyst g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO has a better activity for CO2 reduction to CO than other currently reported materials. The performance is even higher than that obtained from some metallic catalysts such as Cu2O at Au [65], CuO derived Cu nanowire (NWs) [67], Au-CDots-C3N4 [68], and g-C3N4/MWCNT [20], validating the superior performance of our newer one-pot aqueous catalytic system. In electrochemical CO2 reduction,
selectivity is an important parameter because of the formation of complex reaction products. High catalytic selectivity with lower overpotentials (− 0.316 V) has been achieved by non-noble metal catalyst with a moderate selectivity [17]. In comparison to this, our catalyst is found to be highly selective for CO at overpotential of − 0.865 V vs. NHE with a CO/H2 selectivity of 26:1. The reason for this enhancement can be attributed to the synergistic effect between g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO and g-C3N4 as discussed earlier by XPS, XANES and FTIR measurements.
We also measured the work function (WF) of all the catalysts and the obtained WF for the g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO (5.2 eV) was between that of gC3N4 (5.6 eV) and Cu2O-FeO (4.9 eV), indicating a synergistic effect at the electronic levels (Fig. S18). The optimum WF enhances the rate of electron transfer and results in enhanced catalytic activity for the gC3N4/Cu2O-FeO [69]. This synergistic effect was further corroborated by the impedance measurement (Nyquist plot) at -1.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl. The value of the charge transfer resistance (Rct) can be obtained by
G.W. Woyessa et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120052
fitting the electrochemical impedance curve at higher frequency (Fig. S18b). The series resistance (Rs) is similar for all three electrodes because its value is mainly related to the resistance of the FTO substrate and the solution resistance that are kept the same for all the samples [70]. The values for Rct are reported in Table S4, showing that the best Rct value is obtained for g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO, which is 110 Ω cm2, approximately twice as low as that of Cu2O-FeO (189 Ω cm2) and g-C3N4 (254 Ω cm2) indicating g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO has more efficient electron transfer than the other electrodes. These results were in agreement with those obtained from WF measurements [71,72].

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In conclusion, we prepared a novel g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO heterostructure nanocomposite catalyst by a simple hydrothermal synthetic route and tested it for electrochemical CO2 reduction under 0.1 M KCl electrolyte (pH = 6.9) in aqueous systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental report on a hybrid g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO nanocomposite for electrochemical CO2 reduction. The HRTEM images measurements indicated that the prepared nanocomposites exhibited a well-defined mixed metallic oxide nanocluster (Cu2O-FeO) distributed over a horizontal g-C3N4 nanosheet plate with size ~10 nm. The resulting g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO composite catalyst was employed as an electrode and exhibited improved catalytic activity for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction to CO with a small Tafel slope of 116 mV/dec, total current density of 4.65 mA/cm2, overpotential of -0.865 V vs. NHE and a maximum CO Faradic efficiency of 84.4 % at an applied potential of -1.60 V vs. Ag/AgCl. This performance is even higher than that obtained from already reported metallic catalysts. The turnover frequency reached up to 10300 h− 1 with selectivity of ~96 %. This enhancement was due to the intimate interfacial interaction between the g-C3N4 and metal oxides (Cu2O-FeO), the presence of surface oxygen vacancies, and the higher electrochemically active surface area. In summary, we demonstrated that g-C3N4/Cu2O-FeO is a promising electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction in neutral medium. Incorporating mixed metal oxide into g-C3N4 layers could be a potential strategy to improve the electrocatalytic catalytic activity of the composite materials.
